analysis.one_liner: Lets companies calculate pension funding with corporate bond rates instead of Treasury rates, lowering required contributions.
analysis.headline: Senator Judd Gregg introduced the bill on July 31, 2003 and it was sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies that still offer traditional pensions must set aside money each year based on an interest rate. In 2003, with the 30-year Treasury bond no longer being issued, those required contributions had become volatile and expensive. This bill would switch the calculation to long-term corporate bond rates, which are typically higher — so a company's pension debt would look smaller on paper and it would have to put in less cash. It would also create a 13-member commission to study longer-term reform of the rules for these plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers that sponsor defined benefit pension plans — typically large manufacturers, airlines, and steel and other industrial companies — gain the most. Using a higher corporate bond rate shrinks the measured size of their pension debts, reducing the cash they must contribute each year and freeing money for other uses. The bill also gives collectively bargained plans extra transition time before the new rules change lump-sum payouts.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the 30-year Treasury rate with a 'conservative long-term corporate bond rate' for calculating required pension contributions, the current-liability test, and PBGC variable-rate premiums; the rate must come from at least two top-quality indices with average maturities of 20 years or more.

Phases the change in gradually: the corporate rate applies fully for 2004 and 2005, then blends back toward the Treasury rate at 20% in 2006, 40% in 2007, and 60% in 2008, with extra transition protection for workers covered by collective bargaining agreements.

Establishes a Commission on Defined Benefit Pension Plans of 13 members to study how funding rules could increase benefit security, give employers predictable rules, and protect the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation, with a report due December 31, 2006.
Sunsets the rate change: none of the amendments apply to plan years beginning after December 31, 2008, making it a temporary stopgap rather than a permanent rewrite.

analysis.who_pays: If a plan is funded using an optimistic rate and its sponsor later runs into trouble, the shortfall can land on workers whose promised benefits are cut back, and on the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation — the federal insurance backstop financed by premiums from other plans and, ultimately, by taxpayers. Companies contributing less cash today leave a smaller cushion against that risk.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers with pensions and the PBGC

drawbacks.text: Corporate bond rates run higher than long-term Treasury rates, so switching lowers measured pension liabilities and lets employers contribute less cash — which can leave plans underfunded if returns fall short, shifting risk onto plan participants and the PBGC insurance system.

The bill itself directs the commission to examine whether the interest rates used are 'resistant to manipulation,' an acknowledgment in the bill's own text that rate selection can be gamed to shrink funding obligations.
The rate change sunsets after 2008 and defers the real reform question to a commission reporting at the end of 2006, so the underlying volatility problem would return unless Congress acted again.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives employers real, immediate cash relief and some predictability, and its phase-in and collectively bargained plan protections show drafting care. But the relief comes by lowering the measured size of pension debts, not by putting more money into the plans — the classic trade in pension funding law: easier rules for companies today mean thinner cushions behind workers' benefits tomorrow, with the federal pension insurer standing behind failures. The sunset and commission are honest acknowledgments that this is a stopgap, not a fix.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Gregg introduced it and sent it to the Senate Finance Committee on July 31, 2003, and it sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

narrative.text: Senator Judd Gregg of New Hampshire introduced the Pension Stability Act in the Senate on July 31, 2003.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the day it was introduced.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — is recorded for the bill in the 108th Congress.
The bill attracted a single Republican cosponsor and no Democratic cosponsors.
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and the bill died with it under the Senate's rule that legislation does not carry over to the next Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the stricter existing funding rules stayed in place for this Congress: workers in traditional pensions and the PBGC insurance backstop were not exposed to a looser corporate-bond rate, while employers kept pressing for contribution relief elsewhere. Employers gained nothing from this particular bill's death beyond continued uncertainty.

industries.industry: Employers sponsoring defined benefit pension plans
industries.note: Corporate bond rates are typically higher than long-term Treasury rates, so the switch makes companies' pension debts look smaller and cuts required cash contributions. The offsetting cost — thinner funding cushions behind promised benefits — falls on workers and the federal pension insurer, not on the employers.

industries.industry: Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation and its premium-paying plans
industries.note: The bill ties the PBGC's variable-rate premium calculation to the corporate bond rate as well, and looser funding standards raise the risk that underfunded plans terminate and land on the PBGC — spreading costs to other plans and potentially taxpayers. The bill also directs its commission to study how to protect PBGC's finances.
